title: The Verb: Person and the Present
summary: The verb stands last, and it agrees with its subject in person, number and class — so that the division of ¶40 comes back as a set of endings. Telugu distinguishes a true present from a habitual/future, and denies each of them, and the past, in a different way.

rules.heading: The Verb Comes Last
rules.statement: Telugu is a **subject–object–verb** language: the verb closes the sentence, and everything it governs comes before it. The same ordering carries through the rest of the grammar — a modifier before its noun, a suffix after its stem.

rules.heading: The Personal Endings
rules.statement: A Telugu verb ends with a syllable naming its subject. There are **seven** such endings, and they are the same in every tense: the tense marker comes before them, the person after.

paradigms.caption: The personal endings
paradigms.footnote: Seven endings for nine pronouns: మేము and మనం share one, and so do మీరు and వాళ్ళు.

examples.gloss: I went / you went / he went

rules.heading: The Verb Agrees with the Class
rules.statement: The endings of ¶74 reproduce the class division of ¶45 and ¶49. In the **singular**, a man takes **-డు** and a woman takes **-ది** — the very ending a table or a dog takes. In the **plural**, men and women together take **-రు**, and only things take **-యి**.

paradigms.caption: Where the line falls
paradigms.footnote: In the middle row, a woman takes the ending of a book in the singular and the ending of a man in the plural.

examples.note: the same ending as అది వెళ్ళింది, it went

rules.heading: The Present Progressive — తు + ఉండు
rules.statement: For an action going on **now**, Telugu adds **-తు-** to the root and follows it with a conjugated form of **ఉండు**, to be. *చదువుతున్నాను*, I am reading, is చదువు + తు + ఉన్నాను — root, marker, and the auxiliary's own first-person form.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

rules.heading: The Progressive's Own Endings — ఉండు
rules.statement: The endings that appear in the progressive are not ¶74's own: they are **ఉండు**'s conjugation, irregular in the third person non-masculine, where the fuller ఉన్నది has contracted to **ఉంది**. Fused with -తు-, this gives the progressive's **-తోంది** — *చదువుతోంది*, she is reading — a single vowel away from the habitual's -తుంది.

paradigms.caption: చదువు — present progressive
paradigms.footnote: Each piece stays separable, as an agglutinative language requires (¶57): చదువు + తు + ఉన్నాను — root, durative marker, and the auxiliary's own first-person form.

examples.note: ఉంది contracted, not the fuller ఉన్నది

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

rules.heading: The Habitual and Future — తా
rules.statement: **-తా-** takes the place of the progressive's -తు- and marks a **habitual** action or a **future** one. Telugu commits to a single form for both senses, and only the context — an adverb, the situation — decides which is meant.

rows.label: చదువుతాను
cells: I read — habitually; or, I will read

examples.note: the same form, the adverb deciding

rules.heading: -తా- before -ది
rules.statement: Before the third-person non-masculine ending **-ది**, the habitual/future's **-తా-** becomes **-తున్-**: *చదువుతుంది*, never the *చదువుతాది* the pattern would otherwise give. Everywhere else it keeps **-తా-** unchanged.

paradigms.caption: చదువు — habitual/future
paradigms.footnote: ఆమె, అది alone takes -తుంది; every other person keeps -తా- whole.

rules.heading: Denying an Action
rules.statement: An action is denied by a **negative form of the verb**, never by **కాదు** (¶36), which denies an identity rather than an action. The past, the habitual/future, and the progressive negate in three different ways, set out in the rules that follow.

paradigms.caption: The three negations compared

rows.label: habitual/future
cells: చదువుతాను — I read; I will read
చదవను — I do not read; I will not read

rows.label: progressive
cells: చదవటం లేదు — I am not reading

paradigms.footnote: Each denial touches a different piece of the verb: లేదు replaces the past ending outright, -అ- replaces -తా- in place, and లేదు again follows a verbal noun that never conjugates at all.

examples.note: కాదు denies an identity, not an action

rules.heading: Denying the Past — లేదు
rules.statement: **లేదు** is added to the infinitive, which ends in **-అ**, and the personal ending disappears entirely. The form is the same for every person: *నేను వెళ్ళలేదు* and *అతను వెళ్ళలేదు*, I/he did not go, share one verb.

examples.gloss: I went. → I did not go.

examples.note: the same form, whoever the subject

examples.gloss: I read (past). → I did not read.
examples.note: చదువు's infinitive is చదవ-, the same medial change the negative tense makes (¶82)

footnotes: The negative therefore says less than the affirmative did: it drops the person along with the ending.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

rules.heading: Denying the Habitual and Future — the Negative Tense
rules.statement: The habitual/future is denied not by లేదు but by its own **negative tense**: the root's medial **-ు-** ablauts to **-అ-**, and a set of endings distinct from ¶74 replaces -తా-. The non-masculine endings are **-దు** in the singular and **-వు** in the plural, not the affirmative's -ది and -యి.

paradigms.caption: చదువు — negative tense

rows.label: నేను
cells: I do not / will not read

rows.label: నువ్వు
cells: you do not / will not read

rows.label: అతను
cells: he does not / will not read

rows.label: ఆమె, అది
cells: she, it does not / will not read

rows.label: మేము
cells: we do not / will not read

rows.label: మీరు, వాళ్ళు
cells: you, they do not / will not read

rows.label: అవి
cells: they (things) do not / will not read

paradigms.footnote: అవి and నువ్వు share -వు — the same kind of coincidence ¶74 records for the affirmative, falling in a different place here.

examples.gloss: I read / will read. → I do not / will not read.
They (things) do not / will not read.
examples.note: the same ending as నువ్వు చదవవు, you do not / will not read

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

rules.heading: Denying the Progressive — the Verbal Noun
rules.statement: The progressive is denied not by the negative tense but by the **verbal noun** in **-టం** followed by **లేదు**: *చదవటం లేదు*, am/are/is not reading — one phrase for every person. The verbal noun does not conjugate, so nothing here shows number, class, or person at all.
footnotes: Spoken Telugu often contracts this further, to చదవట్లేదు.

examples.gloss: I am reading. → I am not reading.

examples.note: the same phrase regardless of person

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985.

rules.heading: How a Verb Is Cited
rules.statement: A Telugu dictionary cites a verb by its **root** — చదువు, వెళ్ళు, తిను. Everything else is built on the root by adding a tense marker and then a personal ending, in that order and never the other.
footnotes: The root also serves as the familiar imperative: చదువు! is both the citation form and 'read!' to a friend.

examples.gloss: → చదువుతాను, I read / I will read

drills.stem: Where does the verb stand in a Telugu sentence?
drills.explanation: Telugu is subject–object–verb: everything the verb governs comes before it. The same ordering runs through the language — modifier before noun, suffix after stem.
-తు- plus ఉన్నాను is the progressive: the action is going on now. *I read every day* would be చదువుతాను, with -తా-.

drills.stem: Which ending does the verb take when the subject is **a woman**, in the singular?
drills.explanation: -ది — the same ending a dog or a book takes. In the singular the masculine gender holds male human beings only (¶45), and the verb ending is where that fact bites.

drills.stem: Which ending does the verb take when the subject is **several women**?
drills.explanation: -రు, the same ending men take. In the plural the line moves and all human beings are masculine together (¶49) — so a woman's verb ending changes gender with her number.

options: The first is past, the second present.
The first is habitual or future, the second says the action is going on now.
drills.explanation: -తా- covers *I read* as a habit and *I will read*, one form for both; -తు-+ఉండు is the true present. Translating -తా- as a plain English present is the standard error.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly matched?
drills.explanation: వాళ్ళు is the human plural and takes -రు, giving *వెళ్ళారు*. -యి belongs to అవి, the non-human plural — putting people there is the commonest agreement error.

drills.stem: How is **I did not go** said?
drills.explanation: లేదు is added to the infinitive, which ends in -అ, and the personal ending drops away. కాదు denies an identity — *this is not a book* — and cannot deny an action.

drills.stem: **చదువుతున్నాను** breaks into చదువు + తు + ఉన్నాను. Which of these three pieces is the personal ending's own word?
options: none — the pieces cannot be separated
drills.explanation: ఉన్నాను is ఉండు's own first-person form, not a bare suffix tacked onto a marker — the progressive's endings belong to the auxiliary, not to ¶74's table. Root, marker, and auxiliary stay separable, as an agglutinative language requires (¶57).

drills.stem: Which statements about the negative **వెళ్ళలేదు** are correct?
options: It denies an action, not an identity.
It is the same for every person.
It could be replaced by కాదు.
drills.explanation: The personal ending disappears, so *నేను వెళ్ళలేదు* and *అతను వెళ్ళలేదు* have identical verbs — the negative says less than the affirmative did. కాదు denies an identity and cannot be used here.

drills.stem: **ఆమె వెళ్ళింది.** If the subject became *several women*, how many words would change form?
drills.explanation: Two: *ఆమె* → *వాళ్ళు*, and the verb with it, *వెళ్ళింది* → *వెళ్ళారు*. The ending changes not merely for number but for **gender**: she leaves the non-masculine ending -ది for the masculine -రు on becoming plural (¶75). Answering one forgets that the verb carries the gender.

drills.stem: How many **distinct personal endings** does the Telugu verb have, for its nine pronouns?
drills.explanation: Seven. మేము and మనం share -ము, and మీరు and వాళ్ళు share -రు — so nine pronouns are served by seven endings, and the verb cannot always tell you which pronoun was meant.

drills.stem: Which is the correct way to say **she reads every day**?
drills.explanation: Before -ది the habitual/future's -తా- becomes -తున్-, giving చదువుతుంది. The pattern's plain -తా- + -ది would give the unattested *చదువుతాది*.

drills.stem: Which is true of how Telugu denies an action?
options: One negative word, కాదు, serves every tense.
The past, the habitual/future, and the progressive each negate in a different way.
Only the past tense can be denied.
The negative is formed by adding వద్దు to any tense.
drills.explanation: There is no single negative particle for an action: the past takes లేదు on the infinitive, the habitual/future has its own negative tense, and the progressive uses a verbal noun with లేదు. కాదు denies identity, not action (¶36).

drills.stem: How is **I will not read** said?
drills.explanation: The habitual/future is denied by its own negative tense: చదువు's medial -ు- ablauts to -అ-, giving చదవను. చదవలేదు denies the past, and చదవటం లేదు denies the progressive.

drills.stem: Which negative-tense forms are correctly matched to their subject?
drills.explanation: అతను takes -డు, as in the affirmative. ఆమె, non-masculine singular, takes -దు, not the affirmative's -ది — చదవది is not a word. అవి, non-masculine plural, takes -వు, giving చదవవు. మీరు takes -రు, giving చదవరు; చదవండి is the imperative, not the negative.

drills.stem: How is **I am not reading** said?
drills.explanation: The progressive is denied by the verbal noun చదవటం plus లేదు — the same phrase for every person. చదవను and చదవలేదు deny the habitual/future and the past instead.

drills.stem: Across **నేను, నువ్వు, అతను, ఆమె, మేము, మీరు, అవి**, how many different forms does the progressive negative **చదవటం లేదు** take?
drills.explanation: One. The verbal noun చదవటం does not agree with anything, so the same phrase denies the progressive for every person, number, and class alike — unlike the negative tense (¶82), which has seven distinct endings.

drills.stem: Why is **ఆమె చదువుతోంది** correct, and not **ఆమె చదువుతున్నది**?
options: Because ఉండు's own third-person non-masculine form has contracted to ఉంది, not the fuller ఉన్నది.
Because చదువు has no progressive form.
Because ఆమె only takes the habitual.
drills.explanation: The progressive's endings are ఉండు's own conjugation, and its third-person non-masculine cell is irregular: the fuller ఉన్నది has contracted to ఉంది, giving చదువుతోంది rather than the expected చదువుతున్నది.

drills.stem: Match each negative form to the system that produces it.
drills.explanation: వెళ్ళలేదు denies the past with లేదు on the infinitive. చదవడు and చదవదు are both the negative tense — masculine and non-masculine singular — not the past, whatever the -దు at the end suggests. చదవటం లేదు denies the progressive with a verbal noun. కాదు denies none of these: it denies identity.

drills.title: రోజూ
drills.passage: నేను రోజూ పుస్తకం చదువుతాను. ఇప్పుడు చదవటం లేదు — నేను ఇంట్లో ఉన్నాను. నా అన్న ఇక్కడ లేడు — అతను ఊరికి వెళ్ళాడు. అమ్మ వంట చేస్తోంది. కుక్కలు బయట ఉన్నాయి. రేపు మేము ఊరికి వెళ్తాము, కానీ ఈ రోజు వెళ్ళము. నిన్న మేము వెళ్ళలేదు.
drills.translation: I read a book every day. Now I am not reading — I am at home. My elder brother is not here — he has gone to the village. Mother is cooking. The dogs are outside. Tomorrow we will go to the village, but today we are not going. Yesterday we did not go.

questions.explanation: The passage says అతను ఊరికి వెళ్ళాడు, he has gone to the village, and నా అన్న ఇక్కడ లేడు, he is not here — together they place him in the village now.
రేపు మేము ఊరికి వెళ్తాము puts the trip tomorrow; ఈ రోజు వెళ్ళము denies it for today, and నిన్న మేము వెళ్ళలేదు denies it for yesterday — three different times, three different negatives among them.

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage support?
questions.explanation: The dogs are బయట, outside, not in the house. The other three match the passage directly, and set the three negations side by side: చదవటం లేదు denies the progressive, వెళ్ళము the negative tense, and వెళ్ళలేదు the past.

questions.stem: The passage has **కుక్కలు బయట ఉన్నాయి.** If it spoke of the brother and mother instead of the dogs, how many words would change form?
questions.explanation: Two: the subject, and the verb with it — *ఉన్నాయి* → *ఉన్నారు*, the non-masculine plural ending giving way to the masculine one, because people and dogs fall on opposite sides of the plural division (¶49). *బయట* is an adverb and never changes.

drills.romanization: nēnu rōjū pustakaṁ caduvutānu. ippuḍu cadavaṭaṁ lēdu — nēnu iṇṭlō unnānu. nā anna ikkaḍa lēḍu — atanu ūriki veḷḷāḍu. amma vaṇṭa cēstōndi. kukkalu bayaṭa unnāyi. rēpu mēmu ūriki veḷtāmu, kānī ī rōju veḷḷamu. ninna mēmu veḷḷalēdu.
